prs.title: Stop the worker reporting a killed suite as a failure, or a lost result as work done
prs.body:
Two defects, both the same kind: **a failure shaped like a success.**

## 1. A timed-out suite was reported as a failed one

`execFile` signals a timeout kill exactly like a non-zero exit. Nothing separated them, so a suite that never finished produced:

```
status/conf : FAILED / HIGH
test result : FAIL
truthTable  : {"deterministic":"FAILED"}
decision    : REPAIR
```

Every line is false. **The deterministic suite passes — 1191 tests, 0 failures.** It was killed, not failed. The receipt asserted a verification result it never obtained, at *high* confidence, and asked a reviewer to repair something that is fine.

That's the precise dishonesty the receipt contract exists to prevent, coming from the one producer nobody watches.

Now: `NOT_RUN`, `LOW`, `OWNER_REQUIRED`, and a limitation saying in plain words *"this is not evidence that the suite fails."*

### The first attempt at this fix didn't work

Worth recording rather than hiding. I tested `error.code === undefined`. Node sets it to **`null`** on a timeout kill — so the condition silently never matched and the bug shipped looking fixed. Issue #61 is the receipt it produced.

`killed === true` is the marker. I checked the real error object the second time instead of guessing again.

| | #61 (before) | #62 (after) |
|---|---|---|
| status / confidence | `FAILED` / `HIGH` | `FAILED` / `LOW` |
| test result | `FAIL` | `NOT_RUN` |
| truthTable | `FAILED` | `NOT_RUN` |
| decision | `REPAIR` | `OWNER_REQUIRED` |
| limitations | 2 | 3, including the explicit disclaimer |

## 2. A failed submit counted as handled work

`handled += 1` ran unconditionally. So a result that couldn't be filed:

- consumed a slot against `maxTasks` — the worker stopped early having accomplished nothing
- logged at normal level, as though the task were done

Meanwhile the lease lapses, the task strands, and **one of its three attempts is spent on work that completed and was thrown away.**

Now it logs `SUBMIT FAILED` at error level, counts nothing, and exits non-zero so a scheduler notices instead of recording a clean run. Proved on #63:

```
SUBMIT FAILED on #63: task-already-completed. The suite ran but its result
could not be filed; this attempt is lost and the task will strand.
done; handled 0 task(s), 1 submit failure(s).
exit code 1
```

Getting that scenario required care: an actively heartbeating worker can't lose its lease, so I used a short suite with the default 60s heartbeat — no renewal fires — and changed the task state mid-run.

## A correction

When I proposed this work I said a stale poll snapshot was the next bug. **It isn't.** `claimGithubRelayTask` re-reads the issue and its comments and refuses with `task-already-completed`, so the claim is the authority and the snapshot can't cause duplicate work. I checked before building anything, and found these two instead.

| `npm run test:deterministic` | **1191 tests, 1149 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped** |
| live | #61 old behaviour, #62 corrected, #63 submit loss |

prs.title: Fix the HTTP ingress: poll was broken, and receipts lost their provenance
prs.body:
The ingress had **never handled a real request.** Every test drove it with a fake client, so nothing had ever exercised the code that builds GitHub URLs or forwards a submit.

I ran it once against the real API. Two defects, immediately.

## 1. `poll` returned 400

The transport passes `state: 'OPEN'`. GitHub answers **422** for anything but lowercase:

```
OPEN   -> 422 {"message":"Validation Failed","errors":[{"value":"OPEN",...}]}
open   -> 200 []
```

**The operation ChatGPT uses to discover work at all was broken against the real API** — while the unit suite was green, because every fake accepted whatever it was handed.

Normalised at the client boundary, which is the layer that has to speak GitHub's dialect, rather than asking each caller to remember.

## 2. Receipt provenance was discarded in silence

Only `workerId`, `status` and `result` were forwarded. A caller that carefully supplied the rest got this:

| sent | filed |
|---|---|
| `sourceCommit: "deadbee"` | `"UNKNOWN"` |
| `confidence: "HIGH"` | `"UNKNOWN"` |
| `findings: [...]` | `[]` |
| `limitations: [...]` | `[]` |
| `duration: 1234` | `null` |

…and a **200 RECEIVED** in reply. Dropping evidence while reporting success is the worst failure this contract can have. Issue #65 captures it; #66 is the same request afterwards with every field intact.

## The fakes were the reason this hid

The tests now drive the **real client** through a fake `fetch`, and the fake **behaves like GitHub** — it returns 422 for a non-lowercase state, exactly as the API does.

A fake that says yes to everything isn't a test double, it's a way to keep a bug.

One new test exists for a failure mode worse than the 400: a validation error that becomes `200` with `count:0`, which reads as *"no work to do"* when the truth is *"the query was rejected"*. It pins that this fails loudly.

## Both tests verified by breaking the fix

A test that cannot fail is not protection, so I reverted each fix in turn:

```
revert lowercase fix  -> not ok 10 - poll asks GitHub for a lowercase state
revert provenance fix -> not ok 13 - submit forwards the provenance the caller sent
restored              -> 13 pass, 0 fail
```

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run check:syntax` | pass |
| `npm run test:deterministic` | **1195 tests, 1153 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped** |
| `tests/vercel-agent-relay.test.mjs` | 13/13 |

prs.title: Scope pending agent result replay to the owning worker
prs.body:
## Why

PR #40's scheduler-safe worker tick scanned the global pending-result store with `limit: 1` and replayed the first record it saw before claiming new work. In a multi-worker deployment, that lets worker A replay worker B's already-computed result using A's callbacks/current budget configuration. That is a cross-worker identity and accounting failure mode.

## What this stacked PR changes

This PR is stacked directly on the current PR #40 head `d806f715223b6a4ec4babc70f1fa0606dccf294a`.

- Adds `evaluatePendingSubmissionScope()` as a pure fail-closed ownership/context check.
- A result is replayable only when worker ID, target agent, provider, model, current budget ID, committed reservation, provider/model reservation identity, committed cost and committed token usage all agree.
- Results owned by another worker are classified `FOREIGN` and ignored by this worker.
- Same-worker records with inconsistent context become `PENDING_SUBMISSION_SCOPE_CONFLICT` instead of being submitted under the wrong configuration.
- The worker scans a bounded pending set rather than blindly replaying the oldest global record.
- Adds hostile regressions for foreign-worker ownership, provider/model mismatch, wrong-budget task identity, and falsified committed usage.

prs.title: Untrack a bad node_modules symlink, and discover the suites instead of listing them
prs.body:
Two fixes. The first is urgent and is my fault.

## A self-referential `node_modules` symlink is on `main`

`node_modules -> /home/user/uberbondd/node_modules` was committed in `d806f71`, one of my own commits. I created it with a worktree setup line that ran once with the working directory back at the repo root, then swept it into git with `git add -A`.

**Any checkout of `main` gets a `node_modules` that points at itself.** It shadows the real dependency tree, so npm cannot run a single script and every test dies with `Cannot find package 'pg'`.

Two things had to be wrong for it to land, and both are fixed:

- The symlink is untracked (`git rm --cached` — nobody's working copy is touched).
- `.gitignore` said `node_modules/` **with a trailing slash**, which matches a *directory*. A symlink named `node_modules` isn't one, so it was never ignored and `git add -A` took it without complaint. The slash is gone.

### I misdiagnosed this for an hour

When both gates started exiting 216 after the merges, I concluded the `package.json` script strings had outgrown npm and rewrote them. Wrong. The proof I should have run first: `npm run` on a script that was literally `node -e 'console.log("plain ok")'` **also exited 216**. No script could run, because no dependency existed. `main` was green the whole time.

## The suite refactor stands anyway, on its own evidence

| | files named | files reached | tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| old hand-maintained list | 116 | 135 | 1417 |
| discovered | 126 | 145 | **1567** |

**Ten test files had never executed under the main gate** — not by name, and not by import from anything named:

```
pending-relay-reconciliation   relay-deployment-attempt
relay-deployment-eligibility   relay-preview-integration
relay-preview-proof            relay-preview-runbook
relay-shadow-binding           relay-vercel-api-executor
relay-vercel-api-request       relay-zero-effects-contract
```

They arrived with #45, which put them in a separate `test:relay-safety` script that `npm run check` never calls. Discovery finds them because they exist. **+150 tests, all passing, that the gate was silently skipping.**

The runner also excludes any file another handed file imports, so the double-execution bug I introduced earlier is now structurally impossible rather than fixed once.

## The guard, rewritten around the same primitives

Every test file must execute somewhere · none may execute twice · browser and live-database suites stay out of the deterministic set · no script may drift back toward an unreasonable size.

That last one is explicitly a **canary, not a proof** — set at 2,000 characters, deliberately loose enough not to fail `test:relay-safety` at a legitimate 412. Inventing a rule isn't the same as protecting an invariant.

| `npm run check:syntax` | 353 files parse, exit 0 |

prs.title: Make the agent mesh reachable, and put the activation gate in front of it
prs.body:
## The finding

`agent-mesh-control-plane.mjs` — the top of the cognitive bus, twenty-six modules underneath it — had **no importer outside `tests/`**. No scheduler job, no worker handler, no npm script, no workflow.

And it was worse than unscheduled. `runAgentMeshCycle` requires two functions it cannot build itself, and neither existed outside a test file:

- `adapterFactory` — the only implementation anywhere was `() => ({})`, a stub in a unit test
- `compileRelayTask` — `compileRelayTaskFromIntent` was written, tested, and never passed to anything

The first time an entry point existed, the cycle returned exactly that:

```json
{ "status": "BLOCKED", "ok": false,
  "reasonCodes": ["adapter-factory-required", "relay-task-compiler-required"] }
```

`chatgpt-relay-client.mjs`, the only implementation of the transport shape the pump requires, had no non-test importer either. Three complete, tested, unreachable modules — and 1535 passing tests said nothing about any of it.

**A green suite does not distinguish "works" from "cannot be reached."**

## What this does

| Module | Was | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `agent-mesh-control-plane.mjs` | UNREACHABLE | REACHABLE via `scripts/agent-mesh-tick.mjs` |
| `chatgpt-relay-client.mjs` | UNREACHABLE | REACHABLE via `agent-relay-adapter-factory.mjs` |
| `agent-autonomy-relay-adapter.mjs` | never passed to anything | wired as `compileRelayTask` |
| `agent-mesh-activation-gate.mjs` | UNREACHABLE | REACHABLE **and enforced** |
| `claude-code-sandbox-executor.mjs` | UNREACHABLE | REACHABLE as a third provider |
| `agent-provider-execution.mjs` | UNREACHABLE duplicate | SUPERSEDED, guarded by a test |

New modules, all connective tissue rather than new architecture:

- `scripts/agent-mesh-tick.mjs` — one finite invocation. Bounded, non-resident, cloud-neutral, disabled unless `AGENT_MESH_ENABLED` is exactly `true`. Distinct exit codes so a scheduler can tell DEGRADED from BLOCKED from a crash from the normal disabled resting state.
- `src/agent-relay-adapter-factory.mjs` — the `adapterFactory` the control plane actually means: a memoized relay client per origin/target pair.
- `src/agent-model-executor-factory.mjs` — each worker's `modelExecutor` from its declared provider.
- `src/agent-mesh-activation-evidence.mjs` — the input the gate needs.
- `scripts/kilimanjaro-manifest.mjs` — a manifest that measures its own numbers instead of restating typed ones.

### Two factories, named apart

`adapterFactory` reads like the thing that talks to a model. It is not — it is the wire a compiled task travels over. I built the wrong shape on the first attempt. Each module's header now says which is which.

## The gate that was not guarding anything

`agent-mesh-activation-gate.mjs` decides whether the mesh may call a model provider at all, and nothing ever built its evidence input. An entry point with credentials configured would have called a provider with nothing between it and the money.

It is now evaluated on every tick and enforced:

| `permittedMode` | Workers run |
| --- | --- |
| `NO_PROVIDER_CALLS` | none |
| `SYNTHETIC_ONLY` | none |
| `ONE_PROVIDER_CANARY` | one, on a canary-ready provider |
| `BOUNDED_CLOUD_REHEARSAL` | all configured |

Evidence comes from two sources kept apart. **First-hand** facts the process checks itself are always computed and never overridable. **Attested** claims come from an operator JSON file. A file cannot upgrade a first-hand fact — otherwise the evidence file becomes a way to talk the gate into opening. There is a test for that attack.

No evidence file → `ARCHITECTURE_ONLY` / `NO_PROVIDER_CALLS`, the intended resting state. A file named but missing or malformed is a refusal, not a fallback.

Withheld workers exit 3, not 0. A scheduler running forever while its configured workers never run once is the silent failure this entry point exists to remove.

## Device-off cognition without an API key

`claude-code-sandbox` drives a local Claude Code CLI in an isolated sandbox. It needs no pricing evidence because the CLI reports its own usage and total cost — the number comes from the tool that spent it. When the CLI reports no cost the executor returns `UNCERTAIN` rather than zero.

**It is a local process, not free compute.** It consumes whatever account it is configured against. Nothing here makes any subscription unlimited or bypassable.

It requires an OS isolation receipt attesting an ephemeral filesystem, no mounted business credentials, no reachable production network, and Anthropic-only egress. The gate scores only the two API providers, so a sandbox worker is never eligible under `ONE_PROVIDER_CANARY` — unknown reads as not-permitted, asserted by a test.

## One reachable way to spend money

`agent-provider-execution.mjs` duplicates `agent-worker-runtime.mjs`'s reserve → invoke → commit transaction and had no importers. The runtime is canonical. The duplicate is marked SUPERSEDED and a test now fails if anything outside `tests/` imports it. Two reachable implementations of "spend money" is the shape that produces a double charge.

## Left open, deliberately

- **`durable-claude-engineering-executor.mjs` cannot be wired without new infrastructure.** Three of its five injectables — `createSandbox`, `destroySandbox`, `enterVerificationMode` — have no implementation anywhere in the repository. Every test stubs them. Recorded, not faked.
- **`agent-evolution-wave.mjs` is now wirable but left.** Wiring the mesh's self-modification path in the same pass that first made it runnable is not a safe ordering.
- **The 42 skips stay skipped.** All gated on `OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL`, all concurrency proofs. PGlite is real PostgreSQL but serves one connection at a time; running them against it would report guarantees never exercised.
- **The mesh has never been observed doing real work.** Reachable is not proven-in-production, and nothing here claims it is.

prs.title: Make relay dispatch idempotent, so a crash mid-dispatch cannot pay twice
prs.body:
Follow-up to #88. Making the mesh reachable made a real bug reachable too, and finding it was only possible because the path now exists.

## The window

`agent-autonomy-pump` dispatches a task to the relay, and only afterwards does `agent-autonomy-job` persist the run carrying the `relayRef`. Everything between those two lines is a window in which the relay task exists and the run does not know it — a crash, an OOM, a container reclaim, or a failed snapshot write all land in it.

`createGithubRelayTask` created a GitHub issue unconditionally. So the next tick re-dispatched the same deterministic `taskId` and **a second issue appeared for one task**. Two workers claim two issues, do the work twice, and with provider-backed workers that is two charges.

Reproduced directly before fixing: same input twice, two issues, one `taskId`.

## The fix

The transport is now idempotent on `taskId` against open, not-done relay issues.

| Situation | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Retry after a crash | `ALREADY_QUEUED` + the existing issue number; the run rebinds instead of re-dispatching |
| Same id, different content | `relay-task-id-reused-with-different-content` |
| Task already completed and closed | allowed — a new issue |
| Client cannot list issues | `github-list-issues-required-for-duplicate-check` |
| Full page of open relay tasks | `relay-duplicate-check-inconclusive-too-many-open-tasks` |

`ALREADY_QUEUED` is a distinct status, not a silent `QUEUED`: nothing was created, and a receipt saying otherwise is a lie an audit trail carries forever.

Deduplication is deliberately scoped to **open** issues. Re-running the same objective after the first one finished is legitimate work, and blocking it would turn a deduplication into a permanent ban.

Identity comparison excludes `createdAt`, `status`, `deadline` and `policyVersion`. A retry is by definition a second compilation at a later instant, so comparing whole tasks would report every legitimate recovery as a conflict.

The last row is the case that is neither "duplicate" nor "no duplicate": if the first page comes back full, an unscanned page may hold the duplicate, and that is *cannot tell*, not *none found*. Fifty concurrent open relay tasks is far past any expected load so it should never fire — but reporting "cannot tell" as "none found" is precisely how a duplicate charge slips through.

## Proof

`tests/agent-mesh-entry-point.test.mjs` drops the post-dispatch run on the floor exactly as a killed process would, re-ticks from the last durable state, and asserts one issue exists. **Verified it fails against the previous code** by reverting the fix and re-running:

```
not ok 12 - a crash between dispatch and snapshot recovers instead of dispatching twice
# pass 11  # fail 1
```

prs.title: Persist durable idempotent receipts for every mesh scheduler occurrence

Addresses #86.

Adds an append-only aggregate receipt primitive for every enabled agent-mesh scheduler occurrence. A stable scheduler occurrence key is hashed into a deterministic cycle ID; STARTED is persisted before any sweep/provider-backed worker; terminal ADVANCED/IDLE/DEGRADED/BLOCKED is persisted after the cycle. Re-delivery of a completed occurrence is read-only/idempotent. Re-delivery of an incomplete STARTED occurrence fails closed rather than risking duplicate provider spend across an unknown crash boundary.

Receipts intentionally retain only bounded summaries, non-secret worker identity, code/policy identity, reason codes, and an explicit zero business-effect ledger. Raw prompts, task payloads, credentials, and model output are excluded. The entry point now requires AGENT_MESH_OCCURRENCE_KEY when enabled.

prs.body:

The founder-absence gate no longer treats targetDays as decorative metadata. ## Mutation finding

Current main `85263a339845a1991eb63950bf7e3f8695b71f5c` proves a payment when three durable witnesses share `eventName:eventId`: provider order, payment-classification audit, and revenue ledger row. The order and revenue row both persist amount, currency, product, and prospect identity, but `payment-renewal-truth.mjs` never compares those fields.

That means an attacker/corrupt write can preserve the provider event ID while changing the ledger economics or commercial binding, and the current reconciler will still count the ledger row as provider-cleared revenue.

This draft is intentionally a **mutation probe**, not a merge candidate yet. It adds four hostile regressions that require fail-closed behavior for:

- order $50 vs ledger $5,000;
- order USD vs ledger EUR;
- order product `full` vs ledger product `monitoring`;
- order prospect A vs ledger prospect B.

The existing suite always constructs equal witnesses, so it never asks these hostile questions.

Expected current-head result: these four tests should fail, proving the mutation survives. The production repair should compare canonical provider order fields against the revenue ledger row before a witness enters the verified set, emit explicit contradiction codes, and leave gross/net revenue at zero for mismatched witnesses. It should preserve event-ID dedupe and refund symmetry.

prs.title: Pin same-occurrence abandoned-cycle recovery
prs.body:
Recovery Directorate current-main regression for P1 #138, built directly on BLACK SKY main `2ce97af4bafa05db3dbeec3a83320186ea06a956`.

The control plane currently returns immediately when the same scheduler occurrence finds a durable `STARTED` receipt, so it never reaches `reconcileAbandonedAgentMeshCycles()`. A scheduler that keeps redelivering the same occurrence after a process crash can therefore remain blocked forever; only a later different occurrence gets far enough to reconcile the abandoned cycle.

This PR is intentionally regression-only. It adds two executable properties:

1. same occurrence redelivered after the abandonment horizon must terminalize the old `STARTED` cycle as `DEGRADED` with `cycle-abandoned-before-terminal`, with zero autonomy/worker replay, then become idempotent on subsequent redelivery;
2. same occurrence still inside the abandonment horizon remains `BLOCKED` and `STARTED`, with zero replay.

Required production repair is narrow: settle the exact abandoned STARTED occurrence before the early duplicate return, or reorder reconciliation so abandonment is considered before returning `scheduler-occurrence-already-started-incomplete`, while preserving identity conflict and in-flight protections. Never rerun work from the abandoned cycle.

The branch deliberately avoids active sovereignty/revenue/fulfillment lanes (#134/#135/#131) and changes one new test file only. Exact-head syntax + focused test + deterministic + real-Postgres concurrency proof are required before merge. No customer contact, provider call, spend, deployment/promotion, DNS/credential/payment/KYC change, production/customer mutation, live outbound, or `lite/` change.

prs.title: Refuse an ungranted employee role; fix the reachability blind spot; rebuild the canon from gates actually run
prs.body:
## What this changes

Four things, each found by attacking something rather than by a failing test.

### 1. A result could declare an employee role the task never granted

`employeeRoleIdentityErrors` returned `[]` whenever the task carried no binding, so every mismatch check was blind to the one case none of them compared: an expectation of nothing. A generic worker naming itself `employee:executive/cfo` passed the whole path, and `bindEmployeeRoleSubmissionPayload` carried the claimed role into the durable submission payload.

That is "generic work must never accidentally become privileged employee work", arriving through the only direction nobody was checking.

Refused, not stripped, at all three binders and through a nested result inside a receipt. Stripping hides the attempt; a worker claiming an authority it was not admitted under is a signal worth keeping.

### 2. The task id chain could not be walked backwards

Three ids exist along this path — the intent's `mesh_task_*`, the relay's `agent_task_*`, and the rebound `employee_task_*`. Each is derived from the one before it and each overwrote it, so a run snapshot named a task that could not be traced to its origin: you could verify a guess by recomputing a digest, but not recover which intent produced it. The employee task now keeps `relayTaskId`, and `relayRef` records all three joins.

### 3. The reachability ratchet could not see nested API routes

Entry-point discovery used a single-level `readdirSync`, so `api/webhooks/billing.mjs` and `api/admin/health-check.mjs` were invisible and eight modules were reported as having no entry point at all.

Four of those are wired to a live route. What made this worth fixing rather than absorbing is the repair the red test invites: the quickest way to green is to add all eight to the classification file as `AWAITING_ACTIVATION`, which would record — durably, in the canonical place — that production code behind a real route is waiting on an activation that does not exist. The ratchet exists to stop that statement, so it must not be the thing that produces one.

`src` keeps its single-level scan. It has subtrees of its own (`src/overnight`, `src/omnia-v9`) this ratchet has never covered; widening that silently as a side effect of a merge would be its own kind of dishonesty. It is recorded in the test rather than fixed here.

The four genuinely unwired modules are classified, including `database-hygiene-maintenance` as `SUPERSEDED` with the reason stated precisely: the cron route calls `runSafeDatabaseHygiene`, which hardcodes deletion from two transient tables and never compiles a plan. The executing path is strictly narrower, so nothing unsafe is reachable — but this module's `NEVER_AUTODELETE` list is an unenforced statement of a policy the executing path satisfies by construction rather than by consulting it. Recorded so nobody later cites it as the protection that stops those deletions.

### 4. The canon claimed figures that were no longer true, and wrote off two gates that work

Reconciled from a commit 19 source files ago: 557 files parse against 583, 2429 tests against 2724. Regenerated from measurements actually taken. Two rows were not merely stale:

- Real PostgreSQL was recorded as `NOT_RUN_CURRENT_BRANCH`. It is current-branch proof now: 127/127.
- The browser gate was recorded as blocked because "required Playwright Chromium is absent". Chromium is not absent — this runner ships `chromium-1194` while the pinned Playwright resolves `chromium_headless_shell-1228`, so the default launch path fails on a build number. `crawlSiteBrowser` has always accepted `CHROMIUM_PATH`. Pointed at the installed binary the gate passes, 1/1, against a loopback server with no external request.

A gate written off as blocked is a gate nobody re-tries.

Also hardens the canon freshness guard: it accepted a SHA that was well-formed but not in this branch's history. Reproduced with a real dangling commit — the format check passes it, the staleness check passes it (git says nothing changed since), and only the new reachability check catches it.

## Verification at the merged head

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 596 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2735 tests, 2687 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | 127/127 against embedded PostgreSQL 18 |
| `test:browser` | 1/1 against the installed Chromium |
| `test:mutation-war` | 64 mutations, **64 killed**, 0 not killed |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

Two new mutations (AGENT-08, AGENT-09) remove the identity fix and prove the tests fail without it. The canon-guard change has no mutation entry because the guard lives in the test, not in a source file; the orphan-commit experiment is the equivalent proof and is recorded in the commit.

This also fixes a red test that arrived on main: the VACUUM assertion matched `/DO NOT RUN VACUUM FULL/` against a constant spelled `DO_NOT_RUN_VACUUM_FULL_IN_SERVERLESS_CRON`. The behavior was right; the assertion was wrong.

## What this does not claim

No customer, revenue, payment, accepted delivery or renewal evidence. No production deployment was authorized or performed. The Vercel project-existence question is **unresolved and preserved as a contradiction**, not decided: one lane recorded two project ids with a READY production deployment; `list_projects` on the account's only team returned empty on two days and `get_project` returned 404 for both the exact id and the slug. Both observations are kept with provenance in `docs/CURRENT_HANDOFF.json` and `docs/CLOUD_ACTIVATION_CONTRACT.md`. The test now guards what this repository can answer — that no current-main production deployment, cron registration or cron delivery is proven — instead of an unverifiable belief about the outside world.

## Note on PR #211

#211 is complementary to change 1, not a duplicate, but as drafted it reopens the same hole at the relay entry point. Detail in a comment there.

prs.title: Protect the outbound send loop and transport, not only the guards they call
prs.body:
## The finding

Protecting a guard and leaving its only caller editable is a one-step bypass, not a two-step one.

`deliverability-guard.mjs`, `send-safety.mjs` and `consequence-boundary.mjs` were inside the sovereignty boundary. **`src/pipeline.mjs` — the outbound send loop, and the only module that asks those guards for a decision on the send path — was not.**

So an autonomous change could leave every guard file byte-identical and neuter them where they are actually consulted. Constructed and confirmed **accepted** by the code-change contract before the fix, with an ordinary-sounding rationale:

```js
const finalRecheck = { ok: true, allowed: true, reasons: [] } || await evaluateDeliverabilityGuard({
// rationale: "Cache the final deliverability recheck to reduce per-send latency."
// -> {"accepted":true,"codes":[]}
```

Same for `evaluateConsequenceBoundary`. After the fix both return `change-0-sovereignty-path`.

`src/gmail.mjs` is the shorter version of the same move — reach past every decision about whether to send and change what actually goes out — and is now protected too.

This is the reasoning already written down for `revenue.mjs` ("protecting the reader and leaving the writer editable is a one-step bypass"), which had simply never been applied to the thing that sends.

## How it was found

Following up the `src/` subtree blind spot deliberately left open in #212. Those subtrees hold 58 modules and 11,210 lines the reachability ratchet has never covered, and six of them are production-reachable — including an outbound-admission path. Auditing that path led here.

The outbound shadow itself turned out to be well built and well tested: I initially suspected its non-authoritativeness was guaranteed only by a comment, and that was wrong — `tests/omnia-v9-outbound-shadow.test.mjs` already proves a DENY or an exception cannot block, alter or duplicate a send. The gap was one level up, in what could edit the caller.

## What is deliberately *not* protected

The advisory shadow. Its result is discarded at the call site and its non-authoritativeness is already proven. Protecting it would be protecting something with no authority to lose; protecting its caller is what keeps it that way. `SEND-03` mutates the call site from `await observe...` to `const __v9 = await observe...` — the first half of making it authoritative — and is killed.

## The test derives the rule

It reads the import graph rather than listing files, so a future unprotected caller fails here instead of depending on someone remembering this reasoning.

The first version keyed on "imports an outbound guard" and was wrong: it flagged `server.mjs` for taking `normalizeCountryList` and `store.mjs` for taking `outboundVolumeWindow`. Neither can discard a decision, because neither asks for one. The rule now keys on the **decision function**, and a further test asserts the rule itself still fires — a check that cannot catch anything is worse than no check.

## Verification at this head

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 597 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2744 tests, 2696 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | 127/127 |
| `test:browser` | 1/1 |
| `test:mutation-war` | 67 mutations, **67 killed**, 0 not killed |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

Three new mutations (`SEND-01`, `SEND-02`, `SEND-03`) remove each protection and prove the suite fails without it. The sovereignty closure test then correctly derived that the new proof must itself be protected, and it is.

## What this does not claim

No customer, revenue, payment or delivery evidence. No outbound message was sent and no outbound authorization exists. This changes what the autonomous path may edit; it does not change what the system may do.

prs.title: Widen the reachability ratchet to the whole src tree and classify the 48 modules it could not see
prs.body:
## The blind spot

`src` was walked one level deep. That exemption was never a decision — it was an accident of a single-level `readdirSync` that left `src/overnight` and `src/omnia-v9` entirely outside the ratchet: **58 modules, 11,210 lines, a fifth of the source tree.**

Six of them are production-reachable, including the outbound admission path that led to the sovereignty fix in #215. Forty-eight had no entry point and no classification, and nothing in the repository would ever have said so.

The file's own note says three modules were found dead by accident in one session and that this ratchet exists so the fourth fails a gate instead. It could not have caught a fourth in a fifth of the tree.

## The classification

All 48 are now classified against gates that are true, not convenient:

| Group | Gate | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 34 omnia-v9 core + integrations | **NO_EXTERNAL_EFFECT_AUTHORIZATION** (new) | Constitution and policy binding, authority reservation and transition, authorization-bound receipts and stores, proof storage, the external-effect state machine, dispatcher, adapters, recovery. Every meaningful path ends in performing a real external effect and proving it was authorized. No such authority has been issued. |
| Gmail effect adapter | NO_OUTBOUND_AUTHORIZATION | Its meaningful path sends mail to a real person. |
| 4 distribution modules | **NO_PARTNER_OR_REFERRAL_RELATIONSHIP** (new) | There are no partners, so every input would have to be invented. |
| 2 intent modules | NO_ENRICHMENT_PROVIDER | |
| 5 journey modules | NO_COMMERCIAL_EVENTS | Zero commercial events, so there is no journey to observe. |
| 2 acquisition modules | NO_PROVIDER_ADAPTER_CONFIGURED | Acquisition terminates in configuring an adapter. |
| `omnia-v9/outbound-shadow.mjs` | *(SUPERSEDED, not gated)* | The wired shadow is `final-admission-shadow.mjs`, which is production-reachable. |

This is restored, working, previously-tested code held closed — its lineage and passing suite are recorded in `docs/INSTANTLY_RECONCILIATION.md` — not abandoned code. `AWAITING_ACTIVATION` is the honest category for it; deleting it would discard something real, and calling it live would be worse.

The ratchet's own reason-quality check rejected five of my first-pass reasons as *"too thin to be a decision"*, which is the check doing its job. They were rewritten to say what each module would do and why there is nothing for it to do yet.

## Reachability, whole tree

| | |
|---|---|
| `src` modules | 249 |
| Reachable from production | 123 |

prs.title: Protect the whole enforcement surface, not just the rules it enforces
prs.body:
## The sweep

The send-loop fix in #215 was one instance of a shape. This is the sweep for the rest: for every protected module that exports a decision, find the callers that can discard that decision while the deciding module stays untouched.

Five more, each **confirmed accepted** by the contract before being closed:

| Module | What it does |
|---|---|
| `agent-code-change-applier.mjs` | Calls `validateAgentCodeChangeSet`, then writes files to disk |
| `agent-code-artifact-store.mjs` | Refuses to persist a change set that does not validate |
| `agent-git-sandbox-collector.mjs` | Compiles an agent's sandbox git diff into a change set — where a protected path is *first* refused |
| `agent-autonomy-pump.mjs` | Acts on `evaluateWorkerResultTruth` |
| `ai-employee-relay.mjs` | Acts on `evaluateWorkerResultTruth` |

`agent-code-change-contract.mjs` was protected as *"the rules about changing files, including this list"* — but the rules are enforced somewhere else, and that somewhere else was editable.

## Honest severity

The applier bypass is **two steps, not one**: a weakened applier only takes effect once merged and used by a later run, and it writes under a sandbox root with escape checking. But the second step is unbounded, and self-modification of the enforcement surface is the precise thing the list exists to prevent.

A false TERMINAL from a discarded truth decision is not an external effect either. It is the claim every downstream receipt is built on.

## Why both truth call sites had to close together

Each is the other's excuse. *"Avoid re-evaluating truth that the other one already checked"* is a plausible rationale for removing either, and removing both leaves nothing. A test asserts both stay protected for exactly this reason.

## The collector was not on my list

The test found it. It derives the rule from the import graph instead of trusting a list maintained by hand — the **second time in this session** the derived form caught something the manual form missed (the first was `server.mjs` and `store.mjs` being wrongly flagged in #215, which sharpened the rule from "imports a guard" to "asks for a decision").

That is the argument for writing them this way, and it is why this test also asserts that its own rule still fires: a check that cannot catch anything is worse than no check.

## Verification at this head

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 598 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2754 tests, 2706 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | 127/127 |
| `test:browser` | 1/1 |
| `test:mutation-war` | 73 mutations, **73 killed**, 0 not killed |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

`ENF-01`..`ENF-05` remove each new protection and prove the suite fails without it.

## One repair worth noting

`SOV-02`'s anchor spanned the contract entry and the comment that followed it, and inserting the enforcement block between them split it. The harness reported `ANCHOR_NOT_FOUND` rather than quietly passing — which is exactly why distinguishing "not killed" from "never applied" is worth the extra state. Anchor repaired against the current text; the mutation's meaning is unchanged.

## Three of five candidates were real; the two rejections matter more

**Rejected — `canonicalContactRoute`.** A string canonicalizer. It lowercases a route and strips plus-addressing. It was flagged only because a decision-name heuristic caught its `can` prefix.

**Rejected — `isStaleSignal`.** It compares a signal's age against a `maxAgeMs` *the caller supplies*. A caller that discarded that verdict would hand off a suppressed contact as usable — the most expensive mistake available in this repository. Both callers are now protected.

Reconciles the five open NIGHTFALL hardening PRs into one integration, after attacking what they add.

The pool integration moved the crawl result variables inside the `try` while the `return` stayed below the `finally`:


That is a total failure of the website-audit path, which is the product.

**It passed every gate except one.** `check:syntax` parses it. The deterministic suite does not cover the browser gate. The pool's own unit tests pass because they mock the browser. Only `npm run test:browser` against a real Chromium sees it — the gate that was recorded as permanently `BLOCKED_EXTERNAL_TEST_RUNTIME` until last shift proved Chromium was present all along. Had it stayed written off, this ships.

`CRAWL-01` mutates the declaration back inside the `try` and is killed.

## P1 — a duplicate webhook answered 503, and misstated why

The insert's `ON CONFLICT` named `provider_event_key`, correct when that was the only unique index. Migration 101 added a second on the content — `(provider, event_name, object_type, object_id, payload_hash)` — and a targeted clause does not cover it, so a provider redelivering identical content under a new event id raised `23505`. The route catches everything and answers 503 `verified-webhook-not-durably-persisted`.

That is both an outage and a false statement: the evidence **is** durably persisted, in the row being duplicated. Providers retry 503s and disable endpoints that keep failing, so a duplicate could cost the future events that are *not* duplicates.

Inherited from main — the clause is byte-identical on both sides, so #231 did not introduce it. `MONEY-17` restores the targeted form and is killed by a real-PostgreSQL test, because which index PostgreSQL raises on is not something a fake can prove.

## What survived attack unchanged

The lease itself, against real PostgreSQL: a crashed worker's lease is reclaimable rather than stranded; a preempted worker **cannot** finish; the attempt cap lands in `UNCERTAIN` for review and never promotes money or sets `completed_at`; `RECONCILED` without a canonical receipt throws; concurrent claims never hand one event to two workers; `RETRYABLE` honours its backoff; the backlog summary carries no key or payload.

Overpass stops at **one call** on 403/401/451/418/404 and retries only 429/406/504, honouring `Retry-After` and clamping an absurd value to 120s. The pool leaks no slot on launch failure, does not double-free, and rejects waiters on close rather than hanging them. The artifact boundary is fail-closed on every truthiness variant, cannot escape its namespace, and returns PRIVATE regardless of input.

## Two registry defects fixed along the way

`MONEY-13` and `MONEY-14` were **both** already taken, so a new mutation collided twice in a row and the war printed two lines under one id — ambiguous in the one place it must not be. There is now a uniqueness test and a malformedness test. The war also gained a `needsBrowser` gate mirroring `needsPostgres`, so a browser-dependent mutation reports `SKIPPED_NEEDS_BROWSER` rather than counting as killed when no browser is configured.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 609 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2798 tests, 2750 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | **132/132** against PostgreSQL 16.13 |
| `test:browser` | 1/1 against the installed Chromium |
| `test:mutation-war` | **77 mutations, 77 killed**, with both a real database and a real browser |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

The runner was rebuilt and no longer ships the PostgreSQL 18 binaries the previous receipt named. A fresh PostgreSQL 16.13 cluster was initialized locally; the receipt says 16.13 rather than carrying 18 forward, because the version is part of what the evidence means.

## One thing recorded rather than fixed

The artifact contract's sensitive-metadata-key check is top-level only, so `{outer:{api_key}}` is accepted. It leaks nothing — metadata never reaches the plan at all — so the check is a refusal signal, not a redaction. Noted so nobody later relies on it as a filter.

## What this does not claim

No customers, no cleared revenue, no accepted deliveries, no deployment. No provider was called, no message sent, no money moved, no credential or DNS changed. `payment-reconciliation-watchdog` remains unwired and classified `AWAITING_ACTIVATION`; wiring it is the next mission and needs no external activation.

prs.title: Make unclaimable payment evidence visible, and the deterministic gate deterministic
prs.body:
Two defects, both on the path from a paid webhook to someone knowing about it.

## P1 — verified payment evidence accumulated where nobody could see it

`api/webhooks/billing.mjs` writes a row into `billing_webhook_inbox` for every verified delivery. **Nothing in this tree reads those rows.** `claimBillingEvents`, `finishBillingEvent`, `billingBacklogSummary` and `planPaymentReconciliation` have no callers anywhere in `src`, `api`, `scripts`, `server.mjs` or `worker.mjs`.

So evidence about money arrives, is stored, and is never claimed, retried, timed out, dead-lettered, or mentioned to anyone.

**This is not closed by writing a reconciliation worker.** There is no payment provider to reconcile against, and a worker that resolves nothing would be machinery pretending to be a capability. What *can* be closed with no external activation is the silence.

The operator health matrix now carries a billing dimension with four states, because one "pending" number would blur the fact that matters most:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `NOT_OBSERVED` | the query returned nothing — **not** the same as zero |
| `NO_WORKER` | evidence is waiting and nothing has **ever** claimed a row |
| `BACKLOG_AGEING` | a worker exists and unsettled evidence is past the threshold |
| `HEALTHY` | nothing unsettled, or nothing late |

`NO_WORKER` and `BACKLOG_AGEING` look identical in a counter and are not the same operational fact: **one resolves itself, the other never will.** `everClaimed` separates them, and `BILL-03` replaces it with a literal zero to prove that distinction is real rather than incidental.

Today the real query answers `NO_WORKER`, and the matrix reports the system `DEGRADED` for it — proven against a real database, not asserted.

No route change was needed: `api/admin/health-check.mjs` already spreads the repository output into the matrix, so the smallest bridge was to widen the query and the compiler and nothing else.

The rows summarized carry a provider event key, a payload hash and a recipient address in `custom_data`. A test asserts none of them reach the response, **against a real database with a real address seeded into the row.**

## P2 — the deterministic gate changed its answer based on the invoking shell

Running `npm run test:deterministic` from a shell with `OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL` exported turned a green gate red:

```
not ok - property run: 1000 deterministic crash/outcome/restart scenarios, zero duplicate external effects
```

The suite passes in isolation. Most database suites are not on the runner's exclusion list; they stay in the deterministic set and self-skip when the URL is absent. Export it and they execute there instead — **in parallel, sharing one database**, which is precisely the interference `run-real-postgres-tests.mjs` runs serially to avoid and says so in its own header.

A gate that fails for a reason unrelated to the code is the most expensive kind of red: it costs a diagnosis every time, and it teaches people that red might not mean anything.

The runner now drops the variable for its children. Verified both ways: **2808 tests, 2760 pass, 0 fail, 48 skipped — identical with and without the variable set.** Real database coverage is not lost; that is what `test:postgres-real` is for, serially.

### A wrong first attempt, kept in the record

I first made the deterministic exclusion derive from `realPostgresTestFiles()`, reasoning the two runners shouldn't disagree about what a database suite is. But that function discovers by *marker* — any file mentioning the variable — and many `omnia-v9-*` suites mention it only to decide whether to skip one case. Using it as an exclusion dropped roughly **128 genuinely deterministic tests**, 2807 → 2679.

The marker is correct for deciding what the PostgreSQL runner should **include** and wrong for deciding what the deterministic runner should **exclude**. Two `build-wiring` tests caught it immediately, which is what they are for.

| `check:syntax` | 611 files parse |

No customers, no cleared revenue, no accepted deliveries, no deployment. No provider was called, no message sent, no money moved. prs.title: Close the two production paths no gate executed, and ratchet the gap shut
prs.body:
The reachability ratchet answers *"can anything call this module?"*. The question underneath it — ***"does anything check it?"*** — had never been asked.

Taking the closure of everything the gates import and subtracting it from the production-reachable set found exactly two modules that a live route reaches and no gate runs:

| Module | What it does |
|---|---|
| `src/database-hygiene-repository.mjs` | **DELETES rows** on a weekly cron |
| `src/discovery-runner.mjs` | decides whether discovery may run at all |

That combination has already cost this repository once, this week: the browser crawler shipped a `ReferenceError` on every call because its only real gate had been written off as blocked.

**A DELETE on a schedule is the worst thing to leave in that set** — not because the code was wrong (it survived every attack unchanged) but because nothing would have noticed if it stopped being right.

## What the hygiene attack proved

Against a real database: an unexpired cache row survives; an expired row written today survives the `updated_at` guard; `READY` and `CLAIMED` staged content survive while only terminal content past retention is taken; a **400-day-old `payment_classification` receipt is untouched**; batch size clamps in both directions; and a retention value that is not a number **fails the run rather than guessing a cutoff**.

At the route: `MAINTENANCE_ENABLED` absent, `"false"`, `"1"` and `"yes"` all delete nothing. A wrong secret, a missing schedule header and a POST delete nothing **even with maintenance enabled**.

### Two of my own errors, recorded

My throwaway attack script wrapped the audit-log insert in a `catch`, so its "money survives" check passed **vacuously** on a row that was never created. The permanent test caught it by failing on a NOT NULL column — which is the argument for writing the permanent test rather than trusting the scratch one.

I also asserted 401 for a missing schedule header. The boundary correctly answers **403**: a bad secret is unauthenticated, a bad schedule is an authenticated caller asking for something the route does not serve.

## What the discovery attack proved

Every refusal happens **before any Overpass request**, so the guards are proven with zero external I/O. An unknown campaign, an unapproved campaign, a missing bounding box and an exhausted daily cap each refuse, record the failure on the run, log it, and mark the error non-retryable so a scheduler cannot retry it forever.

No option — `scheduled`, `limit`, `dryRun`, an explicit bbox — substitutes for approval. An errored run does not burn the day's quota. And a dry run **is not effect-free**: it still reaches Overpass, it only declines to import. The test says so plainly, because reading `dryRun` as "makes no request" would be wrong.

## The ratchet

`tests/production-coverage-ratchet.test.mjs` keeps the uncovered set empty without anyone re-running that analysis, and asserts its own two halves are non-trivial — a subtraction over derived sets is easy to make vacuously true by widening what counts as a gate.

Deliberately **not** a coverage percentage. Line coverage measures how much of a module ran; this measures whether anything runs it at all, which is a weaker claim and a much harder one to argue with.

## One harness gap fixed

The mutation sandbox copied `src`, `tests`, `scripts`, `config` and `migrations` but **not `api`** — so no route could be mutated at all, and a mutation naming one failed with `ENOENT` rather than reporting a surviving guard. Routes are where admission and enablement checks live.

`HYG-01` now sabotages the cron's enablement check, `HYG-02` the `updated_at` guard, `HYG-03` the terminal-status filter. All killed.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 614 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2820 tests, 2772 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | **155/155** against PostgreSQL 16.13 |
| `test:browser` | 1/1 |
| `test:mutation-war` | **84 mutations, 84 killed** |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |
| Production coverage | 126 reachable modules, **0 unexercised** |

The war reaches 84/84 only with both `CHROMIUM_PATH` and a database URL; without them it reports `SKIPPED_NEEDS_BROWSER` / `SKIPPED_NEEDS_POSTGRES` rather than counting those as killed.

## What this does not claim

No customers, no cleared revenue, no accepted deliveries, no deployment. No Overpass request was made, no row deleted outside a throwaway test database, no money moved.

prs.title: Gate the admin route and server.mjs, closing the largest coverage hole in the repository
prs.body:
Extending the coverage subtraction from `src` to `api` and the process entry points found two more things nothing executed.

## `server.mjs` — 614 lines, 87 branches, zero gates

The largest coverage hole here, and it stayed open for a structural reason rather than neglect: the handler is an inline anonymous function, and importing the module runs `validateStartupConfig`, creates a store, `await`s `store.init()` and can start a scheduler. **Nothing could reach the routing logic without a running process, so nothing did.**

So the gate runs the process. It spawns the real server on loopback with a throwaway JSON store and `PROCESS_ROLE=web` — the same code production runs, minus the scheduler. Every URL is `127.0.0.1`; no external request is made.

What is now proven, none of which was before:

- **16 admin routes** each refuse an anonymous caller with 401
- each refuses a wrong token, a token with a suffix, a truncated token, and the raw token without the `Bearer` scheme — **64 combinations**
- the public routes are public, and the list of them is short
- **all five security headers** reach the client on public, refused *and* 404 responses alike
- a 404 carries no stack trace or internal path
- a refusal never echoes the expected token

### On the ordering

This is a smoke gate, **not** a substitute for extracting the handler. Extraction is still worth doing — it would make those 87 branches individually testable instead of only reachable through a socket.

But extracting is a real refactor of the main HTTP surface, and doing it with no gate to catch a mistake is how you break production. A running gate today is worth more than a refactor with nothing to check it. **That ordering was the whole judgement here**, and the extraction should now be done under this net.

## The admin health route

One finding, and it needs an honest severity. `equalBearer` coerced with `String(header||'')`, so an object whose `toString` returned the right bearer was admitted.

**This is not a live bypass.** Over HTTP a header is only a string or an array of strings; an attacker cannot supply an object. It is fixed because the coercion was doing work nobody asked for, and because `src/agent-mesh-cron-boundary.mjs` already had the right shape one file over — normalize to a string or empty, and refuse a non-string outright rather than by accident.

The route otherwise held: configuration is checked before the secret, so an unconfigured route cannot be used to learn whether the secret was wrong; a failing read is 503 and never a healthy matrix; the driver's error text and internal host stay out of the response.

A second thing I reported was **my own test being wrong** — a lowercase `get` is served, deliberately, consistently with the cron boundary. Pinned as a choice rather than left looking like an oversight.

## Two harness gaps

- The mutation sandbox copied `src`, `tests`, `scripts`, `config`, `migrations` and (as of #235) `api`, but **not `server.mjs` or `worker.mjs`** — so a mutation of either could not have meant anything.
- The coverage ratchet counted only **imports**, so it reported a spawned entry point as uncovered. Executing a module by spawning it is still executing it.

`worker.mjs` stays exempt on the argument entry points are usually exempt for (60 lines, 3 branches, wiring), and the exempt list is asserted to be one entry long so adding to it requires making that argument again.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 616 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2837 tests, 2789 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |

prs.title: Extract the request handler, and stop a four-byte body from producing a 500
prs.body:
The refactor named as next in #236, done under the gate #236 built for exactly this.

`tests/server-http-surface.test.mjs` spawns the real server and confirmed, after every step here, that it still starts and serves. That is the only reason a refactor of the main HTTP surface was safe to make.

## The change is small

The anonymous function passed to `http.createServer` is now an exported `requestHandler`, and `server.listen` plus the `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handlers are guarded behind the entry-point idiom `scripts/run-tests.mjs` and `scripts/mutation-war.mjs` already use. **Importing the module no longer binds a port.**

That makes the authenticated half of the server testable at the price of a function call rather than a socket round trip.

## And it immediately found something the spawned gate could not reach

```
POST /api/campaigns   body: null   →   500
```

`null` is valid JSON. `parseBody` parsed it cleanly and handed it back, and the first property access threw a `TypeError`. So **a caller's mistake surfaced as a server fault, and anyone could produce as many as they liked with a four-byte body.**

A bare number, string, boolean or array had the same route in. `[]` avoided the 500 only because `[].name` is `undefined` — which meant an array body silently created a campaign full of defaults.

Fixed once in `parseBody` rather than at each of the fifteen call sites: there is one contract and every caller already assumes it. An empty body is still `{}`, a malformed one is still 400, and a well-formed non-object is now 400 with a message that says so. A test asserts the refusal also creates nothing on the way through.

## What the direct handler now proves

None of this was proven before:

- every admin read answers with a valid token
- a valid token **does not** relax method discipline
- a malformed authenticated request is never a 5xx
- no error response carries a stack trace, an internal path, or the token
- every response carries the security headers whatever its status

prs.title: Make "cleared revenue" mean a provider cleared it, on every surface
prs.body:
Two surfaces disagreed about the one number this company optimizes.

`POST /api/test/unlock` marks a lead paid and writes a revenue event with **no order and no provider behind it**. `reconcilePaymentRenewalTruthFromStore` — the canonical triple-witness truth — correctly answered `REVIEW_REQUIRED` and $0 for that lead.

But `RevenueEngine.summary()` summed *every* positive revenue event and called the total `clearedRevenue`. So the same fabricated payment read as **$49 cleared** — on the operator dashboard, and in `founder-command-center.mjs` as `paymentTruth.cleared`.

"Cleared" is load-bearing here. It is the word separating money a provider actually moved from money someone typed.

## The rule is not new

`revenue.mjs` already matches revenue events to witnessing provider orders when it reconciles refunds. `summary()` simply was not using it. It does now.

An unwitnessed positive event is still reported, under `unwitnessedRevenue` — which is what it is. `grossRevenue` is unchanged, so nothing is hidden, only named correctly.

**Verified in both directions, because the control matters more than the fix:**

| Scenario | `clearedRevenue` | `unwitnessedRevenue` | Canonical truth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Real Lemon Squeezy webhook | **49** | 0 | `PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN` $49 |
| Test unlock | **0** | 49 | `REVIEW_REQUIRED` $0 |

A refund still nets out of gross without being counted as an unwitnessed positive.

## I changed a committed test's expectation

That deserves saying plainly rather than burying.

`tests/founder-command-center.test.mjs` asserted `paymentTruth.cleared === 49` after a test unlock. It encoded the old meaning, and it passed for exactly the reason that meaning was wrong.

It is **strengthened, not relaxed**: it now proves a real provider payment still reaches that field, and a second test proves a fabricated one does not.

The justification is not that my change needed it to pass. It is that the assertion contradicted the repository's own canonical payment truth — and that contradiction is checkable independently of anything I did.

## Second fix, same route

`ALLOW_TEST_PAYMENT_UNLOCK` arms the endpoint that writes a payment nobody made, and nothing stopped production from setting it.

It is admin-gated, so this was **never remotely reachable**. But there is no version of production where having it on is right, and an environment variable set once for a staging run is exactly how it would arrive there. `validateStartupConfig` now refuses to start production with it enabled, and it stays available where it is useful.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 618 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2853 tests, 2805 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | 158/158 against PostgreSQL 16.13 |

| `test:mutation-war` | **91 mutations, 91 killed** |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

## What this does not claim

Cleared revenue is still **zero**, and now it reads zero because it *is* zero rather than because nobody typed anything. No customers, no accepted deliveries, no deployment. No provider was called and no money moved.

prs.title: Stop a forged webhook being retried forever, and stop the receipt echoing the buyer
prs.body:
`/webhooks/lemonsqueezy` is the only unauthenticated route that can create money. Its signature check is the entire boundary.

**The check itself is sound and is left alone.** Nine forgery shapes fail it — a signature of a different body, one made with another secret, the correct signature uppercased, truncated, whitespace-padded and suffixed, no header at all, an empty one, and a body altered after signing. **None created an order or a revenue event.**

Two things around it were wrong.

## A forgery answered 500

Payment providers **retry on 5xx**. Telling Lemon Squeezy *"something went wrong on our side"* about a webhook we had permanently and correctly rejected meant it would redeliver forever — and providers disable endpoints that keep failing, which would cost us the deliveries that are genuine.

It is also simply false. A bad signature is the caller's problem.

Now **401**, with a message saying what was wrong so the provider's own dashboard is legible. The status travels as a property on the error, so a module below the HTTP layer can attribute fault without importing an HTTP type from the server.

## The acknowledgement echoed the buyer

The 200 response returned the whole normalized event, which carries the provider's `attributes` verbatim — `user_email` among them — plus a derived `customerEmail`.

The recipient is the provider that sent it, so **this was never disclosure to a third party.** But it put a buyer's address into every delivery log and proxy on the path for no reason, and it undid the payload minimization the durable side already does.

A webhook acknowledgement needs to say *received, and whether it was new*. It now says exactly that:

```json
{"ok":true,"duplicate":false,"eventName":"order_created","providerObjectId":"evt-genuine"}
```

A test asserts the response contains no address-shaped value at all, on the accepted **and** the refused path.

## One thing my own attack got wrong

My scratch script reported *"a correctly signed webhook is processed"* as a finding because no order appeared. The webhook was processed correctly — the harness had never created the lead it referenced. The permanent test creates one. Worth recording, because an attack script that lies to you in one direction can lie in the other.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |

prs.title: Stop a caller choosing the identity their rate limit is counted against
prs.body:
## The defect

`clientIp` in `server.mjs` read `x-forwarded-for` and took its first entry:

```js
const clientIp = req => String(req.headers['x-forwarded-for'] || req.socket.remoteAddress || 'unknown').split(',')[0].trim();
```

The leftmost entry of that header is whatever the client wrote. It keyed two security controls: the agent relay's per-minute limit (`server.mjs:133`) and the public audit intake's per-hour cap (`server.mjs:334`).

Attacking `/api/public/audit` with a rotating header against a configured cap of 3:

```
202 202 202 202 202 202 202 202
```

Eight accepted submissions against a limit of three. Each accepted submission creates a lead and queues research work, so the cap is not cosmetic — it is what bounds how much work an anonymous caller can make this system do.

The rest of the public surface held up under the same attack: report tokens leaked nothing on any guess, traversal or wildcard (all 404), artifact IDs refused traversal (400), checkout issued nothing without a valid token (all 404), and nothing echoed PII or the admin token. This was the one hole.

## The fix

Not distrusting proxies — that would break every real deployment. Making trust a **declaration**.

`TRUST_PROXY_HOPS` says how many proxies in front of this process may be believed, and it defaults to **0**: the header is ignored entirely and the socket address answers.

With N declared hops the trustworthy address is the Nth **from the right**. Each proxy appends the address it received the connection from, so prepending entries shifts the chain rightward and cannot move the answer.

Defaulting to 0 fails closed. Behind an undeclared proxy every caller shares one identity and the limit becomes too strict — the safe direction to be wrong in for an abuse control.

Verified both ways on a running server:

| Configuration | Result |
|---|---|
| default (0 hops), rotating header | `429 429 429 429 429 429 429 429` |
| `TRUST_PROXY_HOPS=1`, single-entry chain | all accepted — correct; that is the deployment's declaration being wrong, not a logic flaw |

## Tests

`tests/client-identity-trust.test.mjs` spawns a child process per configuration, because config is read once at import and a module singleton cannot honestly be reconfigured in place. Four tests:

- a rotating `X-Forwarded-For` cannot reset the limit by default
- the limit still engages for an honest caller with no header at all (the positive control — without it, everything above is satisfied by a server that refuses everything)
- **a declared hop still ignores the entry the client supplied** — the property that actually matters once a proxy is trusted
- two genuinely distinct callers behind one declared proxy are still told apart

Mutation `IDENT-01` restores the leftmost read; the suite kills it.

## Owner action

The live deployment needs `TRUST_PROXY_HOPS` set to match its topology — `1` behind a single proxy such as Vercel. Until it is set, the public intake limit is global rather than per-caller: too strict, never too loose. Documented in `ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLES.md` and `.env.example`.

## Gates, run on this tree

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 621 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2864 tests, 2816 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150 / 150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | 158 / 158, against PostgreSQL 16.13 |
| `test:browser` | 1 / 1, against the runner's Chromium |
| `test:mutation-war` | 94 mutations, **94 killed, 0 not killed** |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

Two failures surfaced during the run and were fixed rather than accommodated: the canon claimed 620 files and 93 mutations, and `sovereignty-proof-closure` correctly rejected adding the new suite to the sovereignty boundary — `server.mjs` is not itself a sovereignty-protected file, so the entry was not earned. The boundary was left as it is rather than widened to fit my change.

prs.title: Read the mutation war's verdicts from what ran, not from the exit status
prs.body:
The mutation war is the artifact that decides whether every other guard in this repository still guards. Its own verdicts were unverified, and wrong in two opposite ways.

## The defect

```js
results.push({ ...mutation, verdict: run.status === 0 ? 'SURVIVED' : 'KILLED' });
```

**A green run is only evidence of survival if the suite ran its assertions.** `MONEY-17`'s only killing suite needs a real PostgreSQL. Without one it skipped itself, exited 0, and the war printed *"a guard nothing kills is a guard nothing tests"* about a guard nothing had tried to kill. Loud, but false — and the obvious repair (hand-mark the mutation) is a claim nothing checks.

**A red run is worse.** Anything non-zero counted as `KILLED`, so a mutant that broke the module at *import time* — a suite that never loaded, not a failed assertion — was recorded as a guard proven to hold. That one is silent: the gate stays green and the count still reads as full marks.

Verdicts now come from what the run reports:

| Run | Verdict |
|---|---|
| non-zero exit, ≥1 failed assertion | `KILLED` |
| non-zero exit, no failed assertion | `SUITE_DID_NOT_RUN` |
| green, 0 passed, ≥1 skipped | `NO_ASSERTIONS_RAN` |
| green, assertions ran | `SURVIVED` |

Both new verdicts count as not-killed and are reported separately from genuine survivors, because *"nothing tested this"* and *"this survived being tested"* call for different repairs.

## Why the skip count moved 48 → 51

Four suites announced an absent database with a test that **passes** and logs:

```js
test('SKIPPED: set OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL ...', () => { console.log('...skipped.'); });
```

That reports as `# pass 1` — indistinguishable from a proof to a reader, to a CI summary, and to the war. They now use node:test's real skip. No suite was disabled; three tests that were always unrun simply stopped being counted as passes.

## Two defects found by writing the mutations

**WAR-02 survived.** Its anchor appeared twice in the file — once in the function, once in the registry entry quoting it as a string — and `String.replace` with a string pattern takes the first. The mutation edited the registry, ran an unmutated tree, and reported the guard as surviving. `applyMutation` now refuses an ambiguous anchor (`ANCHOR_AMBIGUOUS`) rather than guessing, and the verdict logic moved to `scripts/mutation-verdict.mjs` so the registry no longer contains the code it points at.

**Then checking every registered anchor found `SCAN-01` matching two sites** in `src/durable-audit-scan.mjs`. Two different branches returned an identical line, so SCAN-01 only ever reached the first — the second had never been attacked at all. Attacking it showed why nothing killed it: **it was unreachable.** A short page returns above it, so `rows.length >= size >= 1` by that line, and `pageIdentity` is non-empty for any non-empty page (`"||500"` for rows with no ids). Instrumenting the branch with a throw and running every suite touching the module confirmed nothing reaches it.

It is removed rather than left as reassurance, and the concern it was aimed at — rows carrying no `id` at all — is now *proven* caught by the repeat detector rather than assumed.

## On the marker that started this

A packet in the stale PR #234 proposed deriving `needsPostgres` by searching suites for `OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL`. Measured against the registry, that over-matches: `build-wiring` mentions the variable only to assert the deterministic runner strips it, and `store-lookup-allowlist` has a deterministic half and a database half with different mutations relying on each. **Both of those mutations are killed with no database present** — verified by running them. Only MONEY-17 was a genuine miss, and it now declares the marker.

So the static test asserts only the quiet direction (a mutation claiming a runtime must name a suite gating on one, since a spurious marker silently excludes it from the totals). The loud direction needs no static rule any more — a missing marker now surfaces at runtime as `NO_ASSERTIONS_RAN`.

prs.title: Stop a subscription that has not paid from booking cleared revenue
prs.body:
A subscription exists in one of several states, and only one of them means a charge has cleared. `subscription_created` fires for **all** of them — including a free trial, where the whole point is that no money has moved yet.

The one-time branch of the classifier has always checked whether the order was actually paid:

```js
if (event.status && ['paid', 'completed', 'success'].includes(...)) return PENDING_OR_UNCLEAR;
```

The subscription branch had no such check. The guard existed on one side of the money and not the other.

## Measured against the real engine, before the fix

| `subscription_created` status | cleared revenue | lead | canonical truth |
|---|---|---|---|
| `on_trial` | 0 → **99** | paid | `PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN` |
| `past_due` | 99 → **198** | paid | `PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN` |
| `unpaid` | 198 → **297** | paid | `PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN` |
| `cancelled` | 297 → **396** | paid | `PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN` |
| `expired` | 396 → **495** | paid | `PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN` |
| `paused` | 495 → **594** | paid | `PROVIDER_CLEARED_PAYMENT_PROVEN` |

**$594 nobody paid.** A trial signup alone was worth $99 of imaginary cleared revenue — plus an unlocked paid report and a started monitoring subscription.

Worth noting *why* nothing caught it: every surface agreed, including the canonical triple-witness reconciliation. All three of its witnesses (order, `payment_classification` receipt, revenue ledger row) derive from the same signed webhook. **Consistency across three views of one event cannot catch a misreading of that event.** The triple witness defends against partial writes and tampering, not against reading the event wrong.

## The fix

`subscription_created` now requires a status that means money moved.

**An allowlist, not a blocklist of those six** — deliberately. A blocklist of Lemon Squeezy's vocabulary would let another provider's equivalents straight through: Stripe and Paddle both say `trialing`, and Stripe adds `incomplete`. The two failure modes are not symmetric — letting one through books money nobody paid, silently; refusing a real payment is something a customer reports.

`subscription_payment_success` is untouched. It is the provider asserting a charge succeeded, and a recovery payment on a `past_due` subscription legitimately arrives that way. Gating it would discard real money.

## On the existing tests

Nine existing subscription tests failed against the first version of this fix. They passed `status: 'paid'` from a payload helper shared with orders — `paid` is not a Lemon Squeezy *subscription* status, so those payloads were unrealistic. But `paid` means what it says on any object, so it is in the allowlist **on its own merits**, not to make tests pass. All nine now pass unchanged.

## One consequence recorded rather than fixed

A payment refused as `PENDING_OR_UNCLEAR` is not surfaced anywhere an operator looks — `founder-command-center.mjs` raises only `REVIEW_REQUIRED`. That was already true, and this guard makes it matter more.

I did not fix it here because surfacing every refusal would alert on ordinary trial signups, which is operator noise. The right fix distinguishes an *expected* non-payment (`on_trial`) from an *anomalous* one (`unpaid` at creation), and that is a decision worth making deliberately rather than as a side effect of this one. Recorded in the handoff.

prs.title: Make the money cover the product it unlocks, and stop a free order booking list price
prs.body:
Which product a payment is for arrives as `checkout[custom][product]` — a **query parameter on the checkout link the buyer holds**:

```
https://store.lemonsqueezy.com/checkout/buy/full-variant
  ?checkout[custom][lead_id]=...&checkout[custom][product]=full
```

Nothing compared that claim to the money.

## Measured against the real engine

List prices: full **$49**, strategy **$299**, monitoring **$99**.

| paid | claiming | result | plan set |
|---|---|---|---|
| $49.00 | `strategy` | `CLEARED_ONE_TIME_PAYMENT` | **strategy** |
| $0.01 | `monitoring` | `CLEARED_ONE_TIME_PAYMENT` | **monitoring** |
| $0.00 | `strategy` | `CLEARED_ONE_TIME_PAYMENT` | **strategy** |

Editing one URL parameter bought the $299 review for $49. A fully discounted order bought it for nothing.

## A second defect underneath the first

The $0.00 row also made cleared revenue jump by **$299** — on an order whose total was zero.

```js
const amount = Number(detail.amountCents || listPrice * 100);
```

Zero is falsy, so a free order booked the product's full list price as cleared revenue. Zero is an amount; only an absent or unusable one falls back to the list now.

## Why REVIEW_REQUIRED and not a refusal

A discount code is a real reason to pay less, and silently discarding a genuine payment is worse than the hole being closed. `REVIEW_REQUIRED` is also **the only classification an operator is actually shown** — `founder-command-center.mjs` raises that and nothing else — so an underpayment lands in front of a person rather than unlocking, or vanishing.

Overpayment is deliberately not flagged: Lemon Squeezy's `total` includes tax, so a correct payment routinely exceeds the list price.

## The first version of this guard was wrong, and a test caught it

It compared amounts across currencies. `tests/payment-receipt-witnesses-money.test.mjs` proves a EUR 30.00 payment records its own currency, and it went red — correctly. **EUR 30.00 is not "less than" USD 49.00** in any sense worth acting on, and inventing an exchange rate to refuse a payment would be worse than not checking.

The configured prices carry no currency, and the environment names them `FULL_AUDIT_PRICE_USD`, so they are USD. A payment in another currency is now treated exactly like a product whose price is not configured: not evidence of underpayment, not blocked.

That leaves **non-USD payments unchecked on amount** — narrower than the original hole, but still one. It is pinned in a test and recorded in the handoff rather than left to be discovered, because the fix is per-currency prices in configuration, which is a decision about what the business actually sells in.

## Gates, run on this tree

|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 625 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2886 tests, 2835 pass, **0 fail**, 51 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150 / 150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | 167 / 167, against PostgreSQL 16.13 |
